brief: Making by hand versus making at scale

slots.titleLine1: Scale is a decision about what to lose.
slots.standfirst: Six things that only survive at small numbers, and what it actually takes to keep one of them anyway.
slots.item1: Why the second hundred is never like the first
slots.item2: The one part worth refusing to automate
slots.coverNote: The last page is the trade nobody puts in the plan

slots.titleLine1: Consistency is the first thing you buy.
slots.body: Every unit being the same is the whole promise of making at volume, and it is bought by removing the decisions that produced the differences. Those differences were most of what people liked and none of what they could name.
slots.v1: Before you standardise it, so the loss is a choice rather than a side effect.
slots.v2: One deliberate variable is enough to stop the output reading as stamped.
slots.v3: Inconsistency in the foundation reads as a fault, not as character.

slots.body: The attention that goes into one piece cannot be spread across a thousand and stay the same substance. Systems distribute standards, not care, and a standard is what care looks like after somebody wrote it down for other people.
slots.v1: Pick the two places attention is visible and give them all of it.
slots.v2: Anything you can specify was never the part that needed you.
slots.v3: Handing off the specifiable part always feels like handing off the work.

slots.titleLine1: Somebody made this stops being true.
slots.body: At small numbers the maker is part of the object and buyers respond to that whether or not they would say so. Growth replaces the person with a process, and the honest version is that the thing people bought was partly the person.
slots.v1: One step that is unmistakably done by a specific person, and say which.
slots.v2: Handmade language over an industrial process is the one unrecoverable mistake.
slots.v3: A line that stays small is a strategy, not a failure to grow.

slots.titleLine1: Small lets you change your mind.
slots.body: Making ten of something means the eleventh can be different, and that loop is where nearly all the improvement comes from. Tooling up for a thousand freezes the design at the moment you understood it least, which is always before the first hundred shipped.
slots.v1: Every week before you tool up is a week of free corrections.
slots.v2: Deliberately short runs keep the loop open at a real cost you can measure.
slots.v3: Otherwise version nine is a rumour and nobody knows why it is better.

slots.titleLine1: Volume competes on the one axis you lose.
slots.body: Anything made at scale is cheaper per unit and there is no version of handmade that wins that comparison. Competing on price is the one strategy fully unavailable to you, which is clarifying rather than tragic once you stop trying.
slots.v1: Do not price against the industrial version. You are not selling the same object.
slots.v2: If the difference is real it is worth money. If not, the price is the smaller problem.
slots.v3: The audience for the expensive version is small and it exists.

slots.titleLine1: Most of it should be automated.
slots.body: The romance of doing everything by hand hides that most steps carry no signature at all and are simply slow. Protecting all of them equally means running out of time before you reach the parts that were actually worth your hands.
slots.v1: Most steps are labour. Two or three are the work. They are not the same.
slots.v2: Nobody has ever noticed which parts of anything were done by machine.
slots.v3: And be able to say exactly why, out loud, without using the word craft.

slots.eyebrow: On the step you keep doing yourself
slots.titleLine1: Name the part you would refuse.
slots.body: One step you would not hand over even if it doubled output. Write down why in a sentence that does not use the word craft.
slots.closingLine: If the sentence is hard to write, the step is habit, and habit is what scale is for.
slots.signoff: Everything else can be a process
